title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
gist: A CDC MMWR study of 2025 survey data estimates 9.8% of US adults (~27 million) used a GLP-1, and 44% of users modified their prescribed use, mostly for cost or availability reasons. At least 23% used compounded, non-FDA-approved versions, whose users deviated from prescriptions far more often (62% vs 36% for brand-name drugs).

insights.claim: CDC researchers estimate that about 9.8 percent of US adults — roughly 27 million people — used a GLP-1 receptor agonist medication in 2025, based on survey responses from over 8,000 adults collected in July–August 2025 and published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
entities: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
insights.so_what: Quantifies the penetration of the GLP-1 market in the US adult population — a key demand baseline for incretin drug makers.
insights.locator: In a study published this week

insights.claim: Among US GLP-1 users, 44 percent reported using the drug differently than prescribed — skipping doses, delaying refills or taking smaller doses — and more than half of those modifiers cited cost or availability.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Price and access constraints are throttling realized volume per patient; pricing cuts or supply expansion could unlock latent demand.

insights.claim: Cost barriers to GLP-1 use are concentrated among younger patients: 58 percent of adults aged 14–39 who modified their use cited cost, versus 20 percent of adults 65 or older.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Younger, less-insured cohorts are the most price-sensitive segment — a target for cheaper formulations and direct-to-consumer pricing.
insights.locator: Cost and access barriers were most pronounced

insights.claim: At least 23 percent of US GLP-1 users took a compounded version, and another 9 percent did not know whether theirs was compounded; compounded GLP-1s mimic FDA-approved drugs like Wegovy or Ozempic but are not FDA-reviewed for safety, efficacy or quality.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Compounded supply captures a substantial share of the GLP-1 market away from branded manufacturers.
insights.locator: Modified use of GLP-1 medications was particularly common

insights.claim: Users of compounded GLP-1 drugs were far more likely to deviate from prescriptions — 62 percent did not take them as prescribed, compared with 36 percent of brand-name GLP-1 users.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Real-world efficacy and safety outcomes from compounded channels may diverge from trial data, a regulatory and reputational risk.

insights.claim: A 2025 study found nearly 40 percent of websites selling compounded GLP-1s stated or implied FDA approval, and nearly 80 percent used brand names in advertising, which researchers say violates FDA regulatory standards.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Misleading marketing by compounders is a potential enforcement target that could curb the compounded channel.

insights.claim: CDC authors call understanding the safety and quality of compounded GLP-1s an important public health consideration and urge research on real-world dose and frequency modifications to guide clinical guidelines.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Signals likely further federal scrutiny of compounded GLP-1s and potential new guidance on dosing.
